## 2. Symbol Analysis

**1. Spiritual Number 18:**

#### 1 + 8 = 9

In numerology, 18 breaks down into 1 + 8 = 9. This simple addition actually describes how the Moon card moves from chaos toward wisdom.

1 represents the "self" — the conscious self, striving to find direction in the fog.

8 symbolizes the powerful, cyclical, uncontrollable forces deep in the subconscious, like tides coming and going, carrying fear, illusions, and suppressed emotions.

When the "self" (1) plunges into this chaotic subconscious current (8), it seems lost, even trapped by illusions. But it is precisely this deep dive into darkness that gives one the chance to truly see oneself. The 9 is the Hermit — the figure carrying a lamp, walking alone on a mountaintop, representing clarity and inner wisdom after settling.

So what the Moon card really wants to say is: don’t be afraid to walk into the fog of your inner world. Those unsettling dreams, inexplicable anxieties, and recurring emotions are not obstacles but gateways to deeper understanding. You have to get lost first to find the path that truly belongs to you. True wisdom often emerges only after facing your fears head-on.

**2. Belongs to the Water Element**

The Moon card belongs to the water element in Tarot, which perfectly matches the rivers, ponds, and the lobster (or crab) crawling out of the water in the imagery. But this water is not a clear stream; it is deep, shimmering, and opaque under the moonlight — just like our subconscious: hiding emotions, memories, fears, some of which we may not even be aware of ourselves.

Water has no fixed shape; it flows and changes with its environment. The Moon card similarly brings a sense of ambiguity: things feel off, but you can’t quite say what’s wrong; emotions fluctuate wildly, easily influenced by the outside world, even misled by your own fantasies. But water is also the source of life. This “deep water” actually hides intuition, dreams, and creativity — you just need the courage to dive in to retrieve true inspiration.

**3. Astrological Correspondence: Pisces**

In astrology, the Moon card corresponds to Pisces. Pisces is the last stop on the zodiac, symbolizing endings, fusion, and spiritual return. It blurs the boundary between reality and dreams — the “danger” you see might just be a projection of your inner fears. Pisces is ruled by Neptune, the planet of fog, illusions, as well as clairvoyance and compassion. So when the Moon card appears, people become especially sensitive, able to sense emotions others don’t express, but also prone to escapism, wanting to hide in fantasies rather than face reality.

**4. Hebrew Letter: The Back of the Head**

In Kabbalah, the Moon card corresponds to the Hebrew letter Qoph (ק), which means “back of the head.”

This image is fascinating — the back of the head is a place we cannot see ourselves, yet it connects to instinct and the most primal life responses. The Moon card reminds us: some fears and disturbances lie “out of sight,” beyond rational awareness, but the body and intuition have already sensed them. It’s like an eye behind you, relying not on logic but on instinct.

Interestingly, “Qoph” also means “monkey,” hinting at imitation and appearances. Just like the moon itself does not emit light but only reflects the sun’s light, the world we see might only be a distorted reflection of reality. The Moon card often brings confusion: what you think is real might be an illusion; what you think is an external threat might actually come from unresolved shadows within.

## 3. Case Studies

### The Moon Card and the Blood Test for Kinship Scene

The core meaning of the Moon card in Tarot is fear, anxiety, deception, and concealment. The fundamental reason people are troubled by these negative emotions is that they harbor secrets deep in their hearts — those unknown, deeply hidden matters they never want to reveal publicly.

In fact, the composition of the Moon card closely resembles the climactic blood test for kinship scene in the TV series *Empresses in the Palace* (*Zhen Huan Zhuan*). The positions of Zhen Huan, Consort Yi, and the Emperor (the chubby orange cat) perfectly correspond to the imagery in the card.

In the Moon card, a wolf and a dog bark fiercely at the moon above their heads. They seem ferocious, but ultimately, it’s because they are scared, fearful, and uneasy! The root of this unease is the secrets they hide in their hearts. The lobster crawling out of the deep sea in the card is also very meaningful — it represents Imperial Physician Wen Shichu, who was dragged unwillingly into this blood test kinship turmoil, trapped beyond his control.

Looking at the two people in this kinship test scene: Zhen Huan’s anxiety and fear stem from her biggest secret — the child is not the Emperor’s. If this were discovered, it would mean death for her entire family, an absolutely forbidden truth to be revealed. Consort Yi’s secret is that she is the mastermind behind this blood test scheme; she had already tampered with the bowl, so regardless of whether the child was the Emperor’s, tonight it would be made to appear “not biological.”

So, facing the Emperor’s expressionless face, Zhen Huan and Consort Yi can only muster all their strength to argue their case, using bluffing postures and refusing to yield an inch — this is exactly like the wolf and dog barking in the Moon card, both using a tough exterior to hide inner fear and secrets.

Also, the lobster emerging from the deep sea corresponds to Imperial Physician Wen Shichu; the turbulent sea in the card corresponds to the Emperor’s continuous suspicion and doubt. Caught up in this storm, Wen Shichu ultimately had to resort to self-castration as an extreme way to prove his innocence and dispel the Emperor’s doubts. This was his only way out at the time, perfectly echoing the lobster’s desire in the Moon card to “escape,” break free from chaos, and prove himself.
